text:
The road came over the pass like an afterthought, a single seam of asphalt stitched between the mountains, and Daniel Voss had been walking along its gravel shoulder for most of the afternoon. He was sixty-two, with a frame gone lean and sinewy the way driftwood goes silver, and he walked these roads several times a month, out from the trailhead where he parked his truck, up toward the high saddle, and back before dark. People in town—what was left of it, the gas station and the diner and the church with the broken bell—thought of him as the quiet one, the widower, though his wife had not died but had simply, after thirty-one years, moved to Santa Fe with a ceramics teacher, which was in some ways harder to explain.

It was late October. The larches had gone gold at the treeline, and the light had that thin, rinsed quality it gets before the first snow. He was four miles from the trailhead when he heard it—a sound like a struck drum, muffled, followed by the long tearing shriek of something giving way. It came from around the bend above him. He stood still a moment, listening the way animals listen, and then began to walk faster.

The car had gone off the outside edge of the curve, where the guardrail ended—the county had been meaning to extend it for years—and had dropped forty feet before striking a boulder. It was a small pale-blue hatchback, the kind young people drive to trailheads and music festivals. It lay on its side, roof crumpled, one wheel still turning slowly, pointlessly, like a clock in an empty house.

Daniel went down the slope faster than a man his age should have, catching himself on saplings, sliding the last few yards on loose scree. The engine ticked. There was no fire. He came around to the driver's side and looked through the cracked window.

She was young. Twenty-five, maybe thirty. Dark hair, a green fleece jacket, a silver necklace resting against her collarbone. Her eyes were half open, and there was a thin line of blood from her hairline, but otherwise she looked as though she might be sleeping. Daniel had seen death before—his father, in a hospital bed in Spokane; a logging accident when he was nineteen—and he knew its particular stillness, different from every other stillness in the world. He reached through the window anyway and put two fingers to her neck. Nothing. He held them there longer than necessary, because there is a part of a person that refuses the information.

He climbed back up and called 911. The signal was faint, one bar. He gave the mile marker—he knew them all by heart—and described the curve, the boulder. Forty minutes, the dispatcher said; the ambulance had to come from the far side of the county. Was the victim breathing? No, Daniel said, looking down at the little blue car. No, she isn't.

He went back down to her.

It seemed wrong to wait up on the road, wrong to leave her alone in the wreckage of her afternoon, though she was past all wrongness now. He settled on a flat stone a few feet from the car, close enough that if she'd been sleeping he could have touched her shoulder to wake her. A jay screamed in the pines and stopped. The sun had dropped behind the ridge, and the light was going blue.

"I'm sorry," he said, which was the first thing, and then, after a while: "I'm Daniel."

He had never talked to himself on his walks, but it seemed important that someone talk—that the interval between her death and the arrival of the authorities not be pure silence, pure wilderness. He thought of the Tibetan monks his ex-wife, Linda, had gone to hear once, how they spoke of the bardo, the forty-nine days. He didn't believe in it, but he didn't disbelieve either, not out here, not at this hour.

"I don't know what you were doing up here," he said. "Heading east, looks like. Maybe over to the lakes. People come from Seattle for the larches this time of year." Through the shattered rear window he could see a duffel bag, hiking boots tied by their laces, a grocery sack that had spilled apples across the ceiling of the overturned car. One apple had rolled out and come to rest near his foot. He picked it up.

"My wife and I used to come up here in October. Linda. Every year, for the larches. We'd pack a lunch and walk the ridge trail. Twenty-nine years we did that." He turned the apple in his hand. "The twenty-ninth year, she stood on the ridge and said, 'It's exactly the same,' and she didn't say it the way you say it when you're glad. She said it like a diagnosis. I thought, well, of course it's the same. That's what mountains do. But for her the sameness had become a wall. She needed the years to add up to something, and I'd always been content to let them just accumulate, like snow."

The light kept failing. He could hear the wind working down the valley through the pines, a sound like water over stones.

"I was a surveyor," he said. "Thirty-five years. My whole professional life was measuring things, establishing where things were. Take a bearing, take another, triangulate, and there it is—the point. Fixed. Knowable. I think I believed life was like that. Establish a few bearings—marriage, house, the walk in October—and triangulate your way to a fixed point, and that would be where you lived." He set the apple down gently. "Turns out the points move. Or the person you're triangulating with moves. Which amounts to the same thing."

He told her about the house in town, the porch that needed painting, the view of the river. About the dog, Biscuit, a yellow Lab whose death he'd felt in a place he'd thought was used up. About the phone call every other Sunday from Linda—civil, pleasant, terrible—where they traded the small news of their weeks like ambassadors from countries that had once been one country.

"She's happy, I think. The ceramics fellow. She sends me pictures of her pots. They're good." He paused. "I don't know why I'm telling you all this. I suppose because you're the first person in a long time who can't leave in the middle." He laughed, a short dry sound, then was ashamed of it, though she was past taking offense.

The sky had gone the deep indigo of early night in the high country, and the first stars were out over the eastern ridge. It was getting cold. Daniel put on the extra layer from his pack, then, after a moment, took off his own wool jacket and draped it over her through the broken window, tucking it around her shoulders. It was absurd—the cold meant nothing to her now. But it would mean something to the paramedics. It would mean she had not been alone; that someone had been cold on her behalf.

"I had a teacher who used to say nothing is ever lost, only transformed. The apple becomes the deer becomes the soil becomes the apple. Then my father died, and I stood there at the funeral home thinking, transformed into what, exactly? Where is he?" He rubbed his hands together. "Now I think maybe the teacher was right, and the funeral home had it wrong. The larch needles are gold for three weeks, and then they're on the ground, and then they're soil. We're the only things foolish enough to think we were supposed to be permanent."

He sat with her a long time without speaking, and the silence was different now—fuller, companionable. The moon came up, nearly full, and the mountains stood around them as they had for a million years, and he understood, with a clarity that felt like weather moving through him, that the mountains were not indifferent. They were simply on a different clock. Everything was on a different clock, and that was not cruelty; it was the condition of all beauty, the larch-gold and the short lives and the long stones.

He thought of the duffel bag, the boots, the spilled apples. Somewhere a phone would ring tonight, and a voice, and after the voice a life rearranged forever around this curve in this road. He said a small prayer for that unknown person, though he had not prayed since he was a boy, and it came out less as a prayer than as a wish cast into the darkness, like a stone into the river.

Then, far down the valley, he saw them: red lights, small as embers, climbing the switchbacks. He stood. His knees had stiffened, and he was cold clear through. He looked at her one more time—the young woman with the silver necklace, who had maybe been coming to see the larches, who had come around a curve on an October afternoon and found the place where the guardrail ended.

"They're here," he told her. "Thank you for listening."

He climbed up to the road to wave them down, and behind him the moonlight lay on the little blue car, and on the gold needles, and on the apples, and on everything that was briefly, briefly here.
